newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rejects Canada criticisms on salmon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rejects Canada criticisms on salmon.

text.p: The United States on Thursday defended Washington state fishermen against criticisms by British Columbia's premier that they had begun aggressively catching Pacific salmon prematurely.
A letter published in Washington state newspapers by Premier Glen Clark "is unhelpful, grossly inaccurate," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said, adding:
"The allegations that he makes -- that the state of Washington has begun aggressive fishing before the strength of the salmon runs could be determined -- are false allegations."
Burns also was cool to Canada's call for binding arbitration in the U.S.-Canada row over how to divide shrinking salmon stocks.

"... We believe that the present configuration of listening to our stakeholders and allowing people who have the greatest stake in this process to be influential in the negotiation of this treaty, that that process should continue," he said.
"I can only tell you that the United States and Canada agreed on a process. And we think it's very important to maintain that process," he said.

Burns added: "So we respectfully suggest, based on this very unhelpful letter that's been published today by Premier Clark, it's time to stop the public campaign and it's time to start serious private negotiations."

Canada and the United States have been holding sporadic talks for the past few months on how to divide dwindling Pacific salmon. But the two sides failed to reach agreement before the start of this year's season.

On Clark's letter, Burns said the United States promised it would conduct responsible fishing this year, and "that's exactly what the people of Washington and Oregon and California are doing -- and Alaska for that part."
He said that Washingotn in fact twice postponed the start of fishery in question until it was clear that the strength of the salmon run justified the opening of the fishery.
The state then stopped the fishery earlier than expected, when catches were higher than originally estimated, he said.

Using a sharp tone unusual between the United States and its neighbour and ally Canada, Burns suggested that "if Premier Clark perhaps might spend more time working on the treaty than writing open editorials to the people of Washington, perhaps we'd make more progress."

The spokesman particularly faulted Canada for refusing to support even the minimum standards for conservation on Coho stocks. This has "made it impossible for us to conclude an agreement for long-term fishing arrangements under these provisions," he said.

Burns argued that the two sides agreed to include their respective stakeholders -- including governors and fishing industries -- in the process of trying to settle the dispute and must stand by that arrangement.

The salmon squabble spilled over into the bilateral military alliance when Clark announced in May that his province was cancelling the lease on an underwater military test range used by the United States.
The Canadian Maritime Experimental test range at Nanoose Bay on Canada's Pacific coast is used by U.S. submarines as a torpedo test range under a Canada-U.S. defence agreement.
But Burns, asked if he took this as a serious threat, replied: "No."
